Emergency liquidity: house sellback $225 + States/Ventnor/greens $500 \u2248 $824, covers NY $600 and Park $500; Boardwalk $1400 already fatal. Do not mortgage States, Ventnor, or greens. Do not trade or fund anyone. p3 is on Chance before Vermont/CT with $0 \u2014 houses must be up before end_turn so $270\u2013$300 forces house sales."}}
message.reasoning:
I am playing Monopoly as player p4 (grok-4.7).

I have $244 cash and just unmortgaged Oriental Avenue. I now hold a light blue monopoly with three unmortgaged properties. I need to choose one action from end_turn, propose_trade, mortgage_property, or build_houses_or_hotel.

I will build three houses on the light blue properties. I will mortgage my railroads and Mediterranean Avenue first to raise cash. I will not buy a hotel because I have no remaining liquidity.

I will mortgage Mediterranean Avenue for $30, Reading Railroad for $100, Pennsylvania Railroad for $100, and Water Works for $75. I will not sell States Avenue, Ventnor Avenue, or the green properties.

Mortgaging the dead assets will raise about $305, bringing total cash to roughly $549. Three houses on the light blue properties cost $150, but the required even building is nine houses at $450.

I will mortgage the remaining dead assets to raise about $206 more. After building nine houses for $450, I will have roughly $99 left.

I can only perform one action per turn, so I will mortgage the dead assets first and build houses on the light blue properties afterward. I am deciding which dead assets to mortgage first. Mortgaging does not transfer ownership, so blocking monopolies remain blocked.

I will mortgage the highest-value dead assets first to raise cash quickly. I need a buffer rather than exactly $450, because zero cash would be dangerous. Player one controls red properties with two houses on Kentucky and Indiana, and player two controls orange properties with two houses on St. James and Tennessee plus three on New York.

Player three controls dark blue properties. Park Place with two houses pays $500 and Boardwalk with three houses pays $1400. That makes Boardwalk fatal if I land there. Player three is on the Chance space.

I am trying to identify which Chance space player three is on. The board has two Chance spaces, and I need to determine whether player three landed on the early one between Oriental Avenue and Vermont Avenue or the later one after Illinois.

Player three is on the early Chance space before Vermont and Connecticut. That means a roll could land on Vermont or Connecticut immediately. Player one will not move until their next turn.

I cannot build three houses on each light blue property now. I only have $244 cash, which covers one house per property for $150 and leaves $94. Two houses each would cost $300, which I also lack. I must mortgage the dead assets first to raise enough cash.

I am ranking the dead assets to mortgage. Railroads are the best first target because they are not a monopoly threat and each is worth $100. Water Works is next at $75. Mediterranean Avenue is last because it could serve as a trade chip for the brown properties, though that monopoly is worthless.

I will keep the green properties unmortgaged. They are valuable blockers and could help me acquire Pennsylvania Railroad from player two. Ventnor Avenue is a yellow blocker that player three might want for a trade, so I will leave it unmortgaged as well.

I will keep States Avenue unmortgaged as a trade chip. I am now checking whether the $99 cash buffer after building nine houses is enough to survive player one's red properties, which pay $150 for two houses on Kentucky and Indiana and $180 for two houses on Illinois.

I checked the standard rent chart. Indiana with one house pays $90, but Illinois with two houses pays $300 and Kentucky with two houses pays $250. Player one's red properties would cost me more than my $99 buffer. New York with three houses pays $600. I cannot afford these rents.

I checked the orange property rents. Two houses on St. James and Tennessee each pay $200, and three houses on New York pay $600. I realized that nine houses would leave me with only $99 cash, which is too little to survive most of these threats. Selling all nine houses would return $225, but I must sell them evenly.

Selling all nine houses would return $225, giving me $324. That covers the $300 rent on Illinois and the $250 rent on Kentucky, but not New York at $600 or Park Place at $500. Even after mortgaging the remaining unmortgaged properties for another $500, my total liquidity reaches $824. That still cannot cover Boardwalk at $1400.

The previous estimate of $600 liquidity was wrong. The actual total is $824, which survives New York at $600 and Park Place at $500. Boardwalk at $1400 remains fatal.

I am now weighing two houses per light blue property against three. Six houses cost $300 and would yield weaker rents of about $90 each on Oriental, Vermont, and Connecticut. Player one currently has $138 cash.

I checked whether the cash figures already include rent payments. My $244 balance reflects post-rent and post-unmortgage amounts, since I paid $90 in rent and unmortgaged for $56 earlier this turn.

Player three has zero cash. They cannot pay rent, so landing on my light blue properties with three houses would force them to sell buildings. Their dark blue properties already have two houses on Park Place and three on Boardwalk.

Player one has five red houses worth $375 total. Selling four would raise $300 to cover the light blue rent and devastate their monopoly. Player two has three orange houses worth $300 total, so selling all of them would pay the same rent. Player three owns five dark blue houses worth $500, which could cover the rent but would leave them with no buildings.

Selling six orange houses would raise $300 to cover the light blue rent, devastating player two's monopoly. Player three has five dark blue houses worth $500 total. Paying the $270 rent there would force them to sell at least three houses, leaving them with only two. Boardwalk could drop from three houses to one or none.

I will not move again until after three other players have taken their turns, so my houses will remain live for the entire sequence. The $99 cash buffer is safe because no one can charge rent to me until I land on them.

I am deciding whether to mortgage all $305 of dead assets or only enough to reach exactly $450. Keeping the full $305 mortgaged would leave me with zero cash after building, but that still leaves an emergency fund of $725 from house sales and unmortgaged properties. That amount covers New York and Park Place, though it still cannot cover Boardwalk.

I will mortgage Reading Railroad first, since it is the largest dead asset. Trading for Pennsylvania Avenue was considered but rejected; player two cannot afford to unmortgage it cheaply, and I lack the cash to develop both green and light blue monopolies.

I will not trade away my light blue properties or chase green monopolies. I will mortgage Reading Railroad first, then Pennsylvania Railroad, Water Works, and Mediterranean Avenue, before building houses.
